analysis.one_liner: Limits Supreme Court justices to 18-year terms with a new appointment every two years.
analysis.headline: H.R. 3544, which would give Supreme Court justices 18-year terms instead of life tenure, sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no action since its May 2025 referral; 86 House Democrats back it and no Republican does.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how Supreme Court justices serve and are appointed. Each justice would serve an active 18-year term instead of for life, and one new justice would be appointed every two years — once in the first year and once in the third year after each presidential election. The nine sitting justices would keep their seats for now but would be gradually replaced: each would step back from active service as newer appointees take the bench, beginning with the longest-serving justice. A Senate that failed to vote on a nominee within 90 days would have to act faster on the next one.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a Supreme Court whose membership turns over regularly and predictably, instead of one where a single justice's lifespan or retirement timing can shape the law for decades. Regular two-year appointments would also lower the stakes of each individual confirmation fight, since each seat opens on a set schedule rather than at random. Presidents of both parties would get a guaranteed appointment cycle rather than facing a Supreme Court that can go years, or a decade, without an opening.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens who live under Supreme Court rulings

how_it_helps.text: Each justice would serve an active 18-year term, after which they would be deemed to have retired from regular active service, replacing today's system of service for life [S2].

One new justice would be appointed every two years — during the first and third years after each presidential election — so the Court's composition would change on a steady, predictable schedule instead of only when a seat opens by death or retirement [S2].
The nine current justices would gradually rotate out: each would be deemed retired from active service, longest-serving first, as each new justice takes office [S2].
A justice filling in during a vacancy would be chosen by the Chief Justice through a publicly transparent and randomized process, rather than by partisan selection [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The nine current justices would give up life tenure, though on a staggered schedule that lets the longest-serving step aside first. The political parties and their allies would also give up something: the enormous stakes of a single confirmation, since a fixed appointment calendar means neither party can bank a decades-long ideological majority by holding a seat open until its preferred moment.

drawbacks.text: The bill changes life tenure by statute, but the Constitution says federal judges hold their offices 'during good Behaviour,' which most legal scholars read as life tenure; critics argue a constitutional amendment would be required, and the bill's approach for sitting justices — they keep the title but not the caseload — would face immediate court challenge [S2].

The appointment schedule is written so it starts from the next scheduled openings rather than forcing any current justice out immediately, which means the current Court's composition — shaped heavily by President Trump's three appointments — would be largely locked in for years until the staggered replacements phase in [S2].

Critics of the bill's premise argue that life tenure is the mechanism that insulates the Court from political pressure, and that converting justices into rotating appointees with a fixed return date could increase pressure to rule in ways that favor future employment or political patrons [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Regular turnover is a real, widely shared reform goal — no other major democracy has lifetime Supreme Court tenure, and staggered 18-year terms are the leading proposal among scholars. The design here has a genuine weakness in how it phases out the sitting justices, which invites a court challenge that could tie the whole scheme up for years. But the downside for ordinary citizens is modest either way: the worst case is that the change never takes effect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on May 21, 2025, joined by 49 fellow Democrats listed in the introduction and 86 Democratic cosponsors in total [S1,S2,S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — has been recorded since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current justices keep life tenure and the Senate confirmation calendar stays exactly as it is; neither party has had to give up its leverage over Supreme Court vacancies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Current justices and both parties' confirmation leverage

for.name: Rep. Hank C. "Hank" Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 3544 on May 21, 2025 to establish 18-year staggered terms for Supreme Court justices [S1,S2,S4].

for.name: 86 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor listed is a Democrat [S3].

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no opposition action — the bill simply has not moved — but all 86 cosponsors are Democrats and none is a Republican, which suggests a party split if it ever came to a vote [S3,S4].

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, but the path is steep: the bill has no Republican cosponsors, Democrats hold a minority in both chambers, and the Judiciary Committee has taken no action in the months since referral. Bills at this stage with one-party support and a majority opposed rarely reach the floor; the most realistic outcome is that it remains in committee for the rest of the Congress. Its ideas could resurface in a future Congress if the chamber balance shifts.
